name: The Investiture Controversy and the conflict of Gregory VII and Henry IV
plain_explanation: Bishops were traditionally invested with the ring and staff symbolizing their office by their feudal overlord (Emperor or king). Gregory VII insisted these symbols be given by the Pope instead, as part of detaching the ecclesiastical from the feudal hierarchy. The resulting conflict escalated to mutual depositions and excommunications between Gregory and Henry IV, Henry's penitential submission at Canossa (1077), and ultimately Henry's later military triumph and Gregory's death as a virtual prisoner of the Normans in 1085.
precise_definition: The eleventh- and twelfth-century struggle over whether secular rulers or the Pope had the right to appoint (invest) bishops with the symbols of ecclesiastical office, understood by Russell as part of the broader project of separating Church governance from feudal control.
why_it_mattered: It was the decisive episode establishing (in the long run) papal supremacy over lay control of Church appointments, even though its immediate outcome (Gregory's death in exile) looked like defeat.
historical_origin: Began over the 1075 dispute concerning the archbishopric of Milan, escalating through mutual excommunication and deposition between Gregory VII and Henry IV.
examples: Henry IV's three days waiting barefoot in penitential garb outside the castle of Canossa (1077) before being received back into communion
Henry's later capture of Rome (1084) with an antipope, and the Normans' brutal sack of Rome in relieving Gregory, who died in their custody in 1085
competing_positions: The Emperor's claim, expressed at the Council of Worms, to be above all earthly (including papal) judgment
influence_on_later_thinkers: The conflict continued, with more moderation, under Gregory's successors, and its later stages recur throughout Chapters XI and XII.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The central church-state conflict of the medieval period.
